Berlin on foot

Wizzy knows 50 places in Berlin, from the big sights to the corners most people walk straight past. Start a walk, put your phone away, and Wizzy taps you on the shoulder when there's something worth looking up at.

A grand square framed by twin domed churches and Schinkel’s concert hall.

The must-sees

  • Berlin Cathedral

    Church · 1905

    Built under Kaiser Wilhelm II to rival St Peter’s in Rome, it was finished in 1905. The crypt holds the coffins of members of the Hohenzollern dynasty.

    Look for: Inside, find the great Sauer organ, with more than 7,000 pipes.

  • Berlin TV Tower

    Viewpoint · 1969

    East Germany built it in 1969 as a symbol of the socialist state. When the sun hits the sphere it reflects a bright cross, which Berliners dubbed the Pope’s revenge.

    Look for: At its foot, find the Neptune Fountain. It stood outside the royal palace until the East German state removed it in 1951.

  • Berlin Wall Memorial

    Landmark

    When the border was sealed in 1961, the house fronts here belonged to the East and the pavement to the West, and people jumped from windows to escape. Steel rods now trace where the Wall ran.

    Look for: The round Chapel of Reconciliation, made of clay and wood, stands where a church trapped in the death strip was blown up in 1985.

  • Brandenburg Gate

    Landmark · 1791

    Carl Gotthard Langhans designed it and Johann Gottfried Schadow made the Quadriga on top; Napoleon carried the sculpture off to Paris in 1806. From 1961 to 1989 the gate stood stranded in the border zone of the Wall.

    Look for: Of the five passages, the widest is in the middle. Until 1918 it was kept for the royal family.

  • Charlottenburg Palace

    Palace

    It began as a summer house for Sophie Charlotte, wife of the first Prussian king, and the district is named after her. It was heavily damaged in the war and carefully rebuilt.

    Look for: On top of the dome, a gilded Fortuna serves as a weathervane and turns with the wind.

  • Checkpoint Charlie

    Landmark

    In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other here for several days. It was the crossing for foreigners and Allied staff between East and West Berlin.

    Look for: Above the street, a lightbox shows a young American soldier facing one way and a Soviet soldier facing the other.

  • East Side Gallery

    Landmark · 1990

    In 1990 artists from many countries painted the eastern face of the Wall here. The best known shows Brezhnev and Honecker kissing, painted by Dmitri Vrubel.

    Look for: Find Birgit Kinder’s painting of an East German Trabant car bursting through the Wall.

  • Gendarmenmarkt

    Square

    It takes its name from a Prussian cavalry regiment, the Gens d’armes, that kept stables here. The French Church was built for Huguenot refugees who settled in Berlin.

    Look for: In front of the concert hall, Schiller stands on a pedestal ringed by female figures of the arts.

  • Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church

    Church · 1895

    Bombs wrecked the church in 1943 and the ruined tower was kept as a reminder of war. Egon Eiermann’s new church beside it, completed in 1961, glows blue from thousands of glass panes.

    Look for: On the steps, a golden crack runs across the ground, set with the names of those killed in the attack on the Christmas market here in December 2016.

  • Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe

    Landmark · 2005

    Designed by Peter Eisenman and opened in 2005, it has no single entrance and no fixed meaning. Beneath it, an information centre tells the stories of individual victims and their families.

    Look for: Walk into the middle: the ground drops and the slabs rise over your head, until the street noise and the other visitors fall away.

  • Museum Island

    Museum

    The museums were built over about a century, starting with Schinkel’s Altes Museum in 1830. The ensemble became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.

    Look for: In the Neues Museum, the bust of Nefertiti stands on her own in a domed room.

  • Reichstag Building

    Civic building · 1894

    Paul Wallot’s building was gutted by fire in 1933, a blaze the Nazis used to suspend civil rights. Norman Foster’s glass dome was added when the Bundestag moved in, in 1999.

    Look for: Above the columns of the west front, read the inscription Dem Deutschen Volke, To the German People, added in 1916.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Berlin and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Berlin passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
